raw_text:
This research plan addresses site variability in completion times for what appears to be identical workflows across a number of businesses. The scope is to determine the measurable factors contributing to these differences and to understand variability better.

Assumptions
The following assumptions guide this research:
- Variability in completion times for ostensibly identical workflows across sites is a common phenomenon.
- Completion times are the outcome of a series of interactions within the workflow and the organization.
- There are observable and measurable factors that differentiate these sites, which we can confirm through our research.

Research design
This research will use an observational method primarily using case studies or comparative design. We will conduct fieldwork by selecting several cases that appear to use the same nominal workflow but exhibit varied completion times. The variation will then be observed directly in the field. After gathering data, we will use statistical analysis to determine the significant factors that account for these differences.

Data or evidence needed 
The data needed include:
- Observation logs to capture all actions and tasks within a workflow
- Time-stamped data on completion times for at least three instances of the workflow
- Documented contextual factors at each site (such as team experience, available resources, site culture, etc.)

Measurement
The flow and time involved in the process need to be measured as accurately as possible. We propose using time-and-motion studies to verify the steps in the workflow and how much time it takes to complete each step under each condition. This will involve documenting the number of people involved, the resources used, and how they are procured. Observers should be trained to use standardized recording methods to ensure consistency.

Analysis
We will use regression analysis to determine how variability in completion times is associated with measurable factors such as team experience, resources, and site culture, using controlling for other relevant factors in the analysis. The type of regression model will be chosen based on the distribution of the data.

Decision / stopping rule
The decision to stop this study will be data-driven, based on reaching our predefined sample limit or identifying criteria that significantly explain the variability in completion times with high predictive accuracy. We will use a confidence level of 95%, which means we will stop the study when we are 95% confident in our findings.

Limitations
While this approach does offer the opportunity to identify measurable factors that account for site variability in completion times, it is subject to the inherent variability involved in empirical work. The field data collected could be subject to observer bias or situational factors that the observer may not have accounted for, but steps will be taken to minimize these limitations
